title: Error Corrections
description: Identify financial statement errors, determine their effects and apply appropriate correction and presentation.
html:
Accounting error versus accounting change

An accounting error occurs when previously issued financial statements contain an incorrect amount or treatment because available information was incorrectly used or accounting requirements were incorrectly applied.

This is fundamentally different from a legitimate change in accounting estimate caused by new information.

Accounting Error

Something in the prior accounting was incorrect.

Example: an expense was accidentally omitted.

Change in Estimate

The original estimate was reasonable, but new information changes the expected amount.

Example: revised useful life.

CPA mindset

Before calculating anything, determine:

  1. Is this actually an error?
  2. Which prior accounts were misstated?
  3. Is the prior period presented comparatively?
  4. What is the effect on beginning retained earnings of the earliest period presented?
  5. What correcting entry is needed?

Common accounting errors

  • Mathematical mistakes
  • Failure to accrue an expense
  • Failure to record earned revenue
  • Recording an asset as an expense or an expense as an asset
  • Incorrect inventory counts
  • Incorrect application of an accounting principle
  • Failure to record depreciation

Prior-period errors

When a material error in previously issued financial statements is corrected, the correction is generally reflected through restatement of the prior-period financial statements presented.

The cumulative effect of the correction on periods before those presented is generally reflected as an adjustment to the opening balance of retained earnings or another appropriate component of equity for the earliest period presented.

CPA trap

A prior-period error generally should not simply be run through current-period income as though it were a current-period expense or revenue.

Retained earnings effect

Because prior-period revenues and expenses eventually close into retained earnings, an error affecting prior-period income can cause beginning retained earnings to be wrong.

Example — omitted expense

Last year, a company failed to record $30,000 of expense and the related liability.

Ignoring income taxes, last year's net income was overstated by $30,000.

Therefore, beginning retained earnings this year is also overstated by $30,000.

Correct Beginning Retained Earnings = Reported Beginning Retained Earnings − $30,000

Correcting an omitted liability

Assume the $30,000 prior-period expense remains unpaid when the error is discovered.

Ignoring taxes and assuming the correction is made through beginning retained earnings, the correcting entry would be:

Retained earnings is debited because prior income, and therefore accumulated retained earnings, had been overstated.

Capitalizing an amount that should have been expensed

Suppose a company incorrectly capitalized a $40,000 expenditure at the end of the prior year even though the entire amount should have been expensed.

Ignoring depreciation and income taxes:

  • Assets are overstated by $40,000.
  • Prior-period expenses are understated by $40,000.
  • Prior-period net income is overstated by $40,000.
  • Beginning retained earnings is overstated by $40,000.

Expensing an amount that should have been capitalized

Now reverse the situation.

Assume a company incorrectly expensed $50,000 that should have been capitalized as an asset at the very end of the prior year.

Ignoring depreciation and income taxes:

  • Assets are understated by $50,000.
  • Prior-period expenses are overstated by $50,000.
  • Prior-period net income is understated by $50,000.
  • Beginning retained earnings is understated by $50,000.

Inventory errors

Inventory errors are especially important because ending inventory affects both the balance sheet and cost of goods sold.

Beginning Inventory + Purchases − Ending Inventory = Cost of Goods Sold

Ending inventory understated

Suppose ending inventory is understated by $20,000.

Because ending inventory is subtracted when calculating cost of goods sold, subtracting too little inventory causes cost of goods sold to be too high.

  • Ending inventory → understated
  • Cost of goods sold → overstated
  • Net income → understated
  • Retained earnings → understated

CPA shortcut

Ending inventory and net income generally move in the same direction.

Ending inventory and cost of goods sold generally move in opposite directions.

Counterbalancing errors

Some errors reverse or counterbalance automatically over two periods if they remain uncorrected.

Certain inventory errors are classic examples.

If Year 1 ending inventory is understated, Year 2 beginning inventory is also understated because:

Year 1 Ending Inventory = Year 2 Beginning Inventory

The error that understated Year 1 income can therefore create an opposite effect on Year 2 income.

Important

Counterbalancing does not mean the original financial statements were correct.

You must still analyze which periods and accounts are misstated when the error is discovered.

Noncounterbalancing errors

Other errors do not completely reverse automatically in the next period.

Errors involving depreciation of long-lived assets can affect multiple periods and may require analysis of:

  • Asset carrying amount
  • Accumulated depreciation
  • Prior depreciation expense
  • Retained earnings

Worked CPA-style error problem

At the end of Year 1, a company failed to accrue $18,000 of utilities expense.

The amount remains unpaid when the error is discovered at the beginning of Year 2. Ignore income taxes.

Step 1 — Analyze Year 1 expense

Utilities expense was understated by:

$18,000

Step 2 — Analyze Year 1 income

Because expense was understated, Year 1 net income was:

Overstated by $18,000

Step 3 — Analyze Year 2 beginning retained earnings

Beginning Retained Earnings Overstated by $18,000

Step 4 — Analyze liability

Utilities Payable Understated by $18,000

Step 5 — Correct the balances

$18,000
—

Accounting changes versus errors

New information changes useful life Estimate Change
Mathematical mistake Error
Expense accidentally omitted Error
Reasonable allowance estimate later revised Estimate Change
GAAP incorrectly applied Error

What you should know after this lesson

  • Distinguish errors from legitimate changes in estimates.
  • Understand the basic restatement concept for material prior-period errors.
  • Determine how an error affected prior net income.
  • Determine the resulting effect on beginning retained earnings.
  • Prepare basic correcting entries.
  • Analyze capitalization versus expense errors.
  • Analyze the effect of ending-inventory errors.
  • Understand the distinction between counterbalancing and noncounterbalancing errors.

quiz.prompt: At the end of the prior year, a company failed to accrue $32,000 of wages expense that remained unpaid when the error was discovered this year. Ignoring income taxes, what effect did the error have on prior-year net income and current-year beginning retained earnings?

choices.text: Net income understated $32,000; beginning retained earnings understated $32,000
Net income overstated $32,000; beginning retained earnings overstated $32,000
Net income overstated $32,000; beginning retained earnings understated $32,000
No effect on either amount because no cash had been paid

quiz.explanation: Failure to record the $32,000 wage expense understated prior-year expenses and therefore overstated prior-year net income by $32,000. Because prior-period net income closes into retained earnings, current-year beginning retained earnings is also overstated by $32,000.

objectives: Explain error corrections and its underlying principles.
Apply the topic to a financial-reporting scenario.
Evaluate common errors and their financial-statement effects.
